title: What is checkpointing in Structured Streaming (`option("checkpointLocation", path)`) — it persists offsets, state, and metadata to reliable storage for fault recovery — and what happens if you change your query logic and restart from an existing checkpoint (may fail if incompatible)?

s1_definition.profdef: Checkpointing in Structured Streaming is the mechanism that persists a streaming query's progress and state to reliable storage so the query can recover exactly where it left off after a failure or restart. Configured with `option("checkpointLocation", path)`, the checkpoint directory stores the source offsets that have been read, the committed offsets that have been fully processed, the contents of the state store for stateful queries, and query metadata. On restart Spark reads the checkpoint, resumes from the last committed offsets, and restores the state, which is what delivers exactly-once processing. If you change the query logic in an incompatible way and restart from the same checkpoint, Spark may refuse to start because the saved plan or state schema no longer matches the new query.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India the checkpoint is like a continuously updated logbook that records exactly which transaction slips have been read, which have been fully posted, and the current running tallies. If the clerk collapses mid-shift, a replacement reads the logbook, sees precisely where to resume, and recovers the tallies, so no slip is double-posted or skipped. But if you rewrite the whole posting procedure and then hand the replacement the old logbook, the entries may no longer make sense under the new procedure, and the replacement refuses to continue to avoid corrupting the books.
s1_definition.oneliner: The checkpoint persists read offsets, committed offsets, state, and metadata to reliable storage so a streaming query resumes exactly-once — but incompatible query changes can make an existing checkpoint unusable.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Checkpointing in Structured Streaming is the mechanism that persists a streaming query's progress and state to reliable storage so the query can recover exactly where it left off after a failure or restart. Configured with `option("checkpointLocation", path)`, the checkpoint directory stores the source offsets that have been read, the committed offsets that have been fully processed, the contents of the state store for stateful queries, and query metadata. On restart Spark reads the checkpoint, resumes from the last committed offsets, and restores the state, which is what delivers exactly-once processing. If you change the query logic in an incompatible way and restart from the same checkpoint, Spark may refuse to start because the saved plan or state schema no longer matches the new query.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India the checkpoint is like a continuously updated logbook that records exactly which transaction slips have been read, which have been fully posted, and the current running tallies. If the clerk collapses mid-shift, a replacement reads the logbook, sees precisely where to resume, and recovers the tallies, so no slip is double-posted or skipped. But if you rewrite the whole posting procedure and then hand the replacement the old logbook, the entries may no longer make sense under the new procedure, and the replacement refuses to continue to avoid corrupting the books.

**One line to remember:** The checkpoint persists read offsets, committed offsets, state, and metadata to reliable storage so a streaming query resumes exactly-once — but incompatible query changes can make an existing checkpoint unusable.

sections.s2_technical:
The checkpoint location must be on reliable, durable storage such as HDFS or S3, not local disk, because it has to survive the loss of any single executor or the driver. You set it once per query with `writeStream.option("checkpointLocation", path)`, and every streaming query needs its own distinct path; sharing one path between two queries corrupts both. The directory contains several subfolders: offsets (the range read in each batch), commits (batches fully processed), the state store (for stateful operations), and metadata about the query id.

Offset tracking is what gives at-least-once and, with idempotent sinks, exactly-once. Before processing a batch, Spark writes the offset range it is about to read to the offsets log — this is write-ahead. After the batch is fully processed and written to the sink, Spark writes to the commits log. On restart Spark looks at the last offsets entry and the last commits entry: if a batch was started but not committed, it reprocesses that batch, and because the sink is idempotent or transactional, reprocessing does not duplicate output. This is how exactly-once survives a crash.

State recovery applies to stateful queries. The state store for windowed aggregations, joins, and deduplication is versioned per batch and written into the checkpoint. On restart Spark restores the state as of the last committed batch, so running counts and buffered join rows continue from where they were rather than resetting to zero. Without the checkpointed state, a stateful query could not recover correctly.

Incompatible changes are the main operational hazard. Spark records the query plan and the state schema in the checkpoint. Some changes are safe across restarts, such as adjusting a non-stateful filter value or changing the trigger interval. Others are unsafe and cause a failure or wrong results on restart, such as changing the aggregation keys, altering the state schema, changing the number of stateful operators, or switching output mode in a way the saved plan does not allow. When you make such a change you must start from a fresh checkpoint, which means reprocessing or accepting a state reset.

A senior-level nuance is managing checkpoints as part of deployment. Because an incompatible change requires a new checkpoint, teams version their checkpoint paths and plan migrations deliberately: for a breaking change they may run the new query against a new checkpoint while backfilling, rather than pointing it at the old one and hoping. They also monitor checkpoint write latency, because for large state the per-batch checkpoint write can dominate batch duration, and they choose the RocksDB state store and tune checkpoint intervals to keep that cost manageable. Treating the checkpoint as durable, query-specific, and sensitive to logic changes is essential to running streaming reliably in production.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs a streaming per-account count. If the job crashes, it must resume from the last committed batch with its running counts intact, not restart from zero and not reprocess already-committed batches. This is offset plus state recovery from the checkpoint.

Problem 2 — A deployment changes the aggregation to group by a different key. Restarting from the old checkpoint would be incompatible because the state schema changed, so Spark should refuse and the team must use a fresh checkpoint.

Problem 3 — A safe change adjusts only the trigger interval. Restarting from the existing checkpoint is fine because the stateful plan is unchanged.

The demo simulates a checkpoint as a small persisted record of committed offset and running state, shows recovery after a simulated crash, and shows a compatibility check that rejects an incompatible query change while accepting a safe one.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a checkpoint at committed offset 5 with running counts SAV2001 equals 12 and CUR3001 equals 7, under the state schema groupBy on accountId.

Step 1: The checkpoint is saved. The manager stores the committed offset, the state map, and the schema id, standing in for the write to durable S3 storage.

Step 2: A crash is simulated and the same query restarts. Recovery reads the checkpoint, so the job resumes after offset 5 with the counts intact — it neither reprocesses committed batches nor resets state, which is exactly-once recovery.

Step 3: A safe restart is checked. The new query keeps the same groupBy-on-accountId schema (only the trigger interval changed), so the compatibility check returns true and the restart from the existing checkpoint is allowed.

Step 4: A breaking restart is checked. The new query groups by branchCode, a different state schema, so the compatibility check returns false and logs a severe message instructing the team to use a fresh checkpoint rather than corrupt recovery.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 05:15:00 INFO    Checkpoint saved: offset=5 state={SAV2001=12, CUR3001=7} schema=groupBy:accountId
2026-10-30 05:15:00 INFO    --- simulated crash, restarting same query ---
2026-10-30 05:15:00 INFO    Recovered from offset 5 with state {SAV2001=12, CUR3001=7}
2026-10-30 05:15:00 INFO    Resuming after offset 5 (no reprocessing of committed batches, state intact)
2026-10-30 05:15:00 INFO    Restart with trigger-only change compatible? true
2026-10-30 05:15:00 SEVERE  Incompatible restart: checkpoint schema 'groupBy:accountId' != new schema 'groupBy:branchCode' — use a fresh checkpoint
2026-10-30 05:15:00 INFO    Restart with new grouping key compatible? false → must use a fresh checkpoint
2026-10-30 05:15:00 INFO    Checkpoint demo complete.
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Streaming query (per-account count)
    │ each batch: write-ahead offsets → process → commit
    ▼
  Checkpoint (durable: HDFS/S3)
    ├─ offsets log   (range read)
    ├─ commits log   (batches done)
    ├─ state store   ({SAV2001=12, CUR3001=7})
    └─ metadata      (query id, state schema)
    │
    ├─ CRASH + restart (same query) ─→ recover offset 5 + state ─→ exactly-once resume
    │
    ├─ restart (trigger change)      ─→ schema matches ─→ ALLOWED
    │
    └─ restart (new grouping key)    ─→ schema differs ─→ REJECTED (fresh checkpoint)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Checkpointing in Structured Streaming is the mechanism that persists a query's progress and state to reliable storage so it can recover exactly where it left off. You configure it with the checkpointLocation option pointing at durable storage like HDFS or S3, and the checkpoint directory stores the offsets read, the offsets committed, the state store for stateful operations, and query metadata. Each batch is written ahead before processing and committed after the sink write, so on restart Spark reprocesses only a batch that was started but not committed, and because the sink is idempotent or transactional, that reprocessing does not duplicate output — this is how it delivers exactly-once across a crash. For stateful queries the state store is restored from the checkpoint so running counts and buffered join rows continue rather than resetting.

The main operational hazard is changing the query logic and restarting from an existing checkpoint. Spark records the plan and the state schema, so some changes are safe across restarts, like adjusting a non-stateful filter value or the trigger interval, while others are incompatible — changing aggregation keys, altering the state schema, or changing the number of stateful operators — and cause the restart to fail or produce wrong results. For a breaking change you must start from a fresh checkpoint, which means reprocessing or accepting a state reset.

At the National Bank of India I treated checkpoints as durable, query-specific, and sensitive to logic changes. Every streaming query had its own S3 checkpoint path, never shared, and after a crash the per-account count job resumed from the last committed batch with its running counts intact. When a deployment changed the aggregation key we deliberately pointed the new query at a new checkpoint path and backfilled, rather than reusing the old one and risking corruption, and for large state we used the RocksDB state store and monitored checkpoint write latency because it can dominate batch time. In interviews I summarize it as: the checkpoint persists offsets, state, and metadata for exactly-once recovery, must live on durable storage with one path per query, and will reject an incompatible query change — so plan checkpoint migrations as part of every breaking deployment.
